other_side: NLW reads the wave of inference cost cuts — OpenAI's undisclosed 50 percent trick, founders reporting 75 percent savings overnight, Base44 rolling its own model — as the industry engineering its way out of the compute crunch, a bullish sign. Zitron argues the exact opposite: nobody has ever shown the labs are actually profitable on inference, and cheaper tokens do not fix that. He notes Anthropic's own March affidavit implies it spent roughly three dollars of compute for every dollar of revenue, that Coatue found 85 percent of its 2025 revenue was API calls yet it still loses money, and that subscriptions let users "burn between $8 and $13.50 of every dollar." His conclusion: "If the margins were good, they'd be sharing the margins." Falling inference costs, to him, are a race to subsidise demand, not a path to sustainability.
truth_beneath: Both men orbit one variable: whether the cost of running these models can fall to genuinely unsubsidised profitability, or whether cheaper inference is just subsidy in a new suit. Both accept that token prices are collapsing fast and that the leading labs still post enormous losses. The empirical question is whether falling unit costs actually reach positive gross margin on real, paid usage; the observable that settles it is an audited inference margin — cost per token served against price charged — disclosed rather than asserted. The residue is worldview: NLW reads a 50 percent efficiency trick as engineering escaping the crunch, Zitron reads the same figure as proof they must keep cutting because the economics never worked. NLW is vindicated if a lab publishes real inference profit; Zitron if capex and compute deals keep outrunning it. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain with a paid newsletter — and the signal is where they agree: prices are falling. Watch whether any lab discloses an audited inference margin rather than a run rate.
